title: US growth is being reconfigured by fiscal stimulus, tariffs, immigration, aging, and AI investment
source_unit: Congressional Budget Office The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2026 to 2036
geography: United States; federal budget, macroeconomy, labor force, households, firms, trade, and global exposure

denominator.unit: annual real GDP growth comparison frame

real_gdp_growth_2026.unit: percent projected real GDP growth in 2026

real_gdp_growth_2027.unit: percent projected real GDP growth in 2027

growth_2027_2036.unit: average annual percent real GDP growth projected from 2027 through 2036

inflation_2030.unit: percent PCE inflation projected around 2030 and thereafter

observations.method: CBO baseline projections incorporating enacted law, implemented tariff and immigration policies, fiscal changes, labor-force projections, and macroeconomic assumptions.
observations.uncertainty: These are baseline forecasts, not observed outcomes; CBO emphasizes uncertainty around policy effects, tariffs, immigration, AI diffusion, geopolitical conflict, interest rates, and global demand.
observations.subgroup: US households, workers, firms, governments, and trading partners affected by the macroeconomic baseline.
observations.counterinterpretation: Near-term growth can improve while longer-run growth slows; aggregate GDP and inflation do not establish equal household purchasing power, regional outcomes, or distributional welfare.

observations.period: 2026 and later; fiscal and trade-policy interaction

reconciliation_act.value: boosts near-term consumer spending and private investment and raises productive capacity through labor supply and investment effects

tariff_effect.value: higher tariffs raise imported-goods costs, reduce purchasing power, reduce foreign investment, and lower economic efficiency

tariff_inflation.value: inflation is projected higher through 2029 than in the January 2025 forecast, primarily because of higher tariffs

deficits.unit: trillion dollars in projected federal deficits from 2026 through 2035

observations.method: CBO comparison of its current baseline with prior projections and decomposition of enacted fiscal, tariff, and immigration-policy effects.
observations.uncertainty: The effects are model-based estimates conditional on current law and CBO assumptions; they do not predict the incidence of costs and gains across specific households, sectors, or regions.
observations.subgroup: Consumers of imported goods, workers, firms using imported inputs, investors, taxpayers, recipients of federal programs, and trading partners.
observations.counterinterpretation: Tariffs can redirect production and supply chains and fiscal changes can increase investment; the report's projected aggregate drag does not mean every industry or household experiences a loss.

denominator.unit: civilian noninstitutionalized population and labor-force projection frame

payroll_growth.unit: average jobs added per month projected from 2028 through 2036

labor_supply_drivers.value: population aging and reduced net immigration slow labor-force growth

observations.method: CBO labor-market and demographic projections using population, immigration, participation, employment, and policy assumptions.
observations.uncertainty: Labor-force projections depend on fertility, mortality, migration, participation, policy implementation, business demand, and future technological change; they are not a forecast of any person's employment path.
observations.subgroup: Workers, employers, immigrants, older adults, younger entrants, caregivers, and regions with differing demographic structures.
observations.counterinterpretation: A declining participation rate can coexist with low unemployment and productivity growth; labor scarcity may raise wages or accelerate automation in some sectors while reducing opportunity in others.

observations.period: 2026-2036; trade, dollar, AI, and productive-capacity pathway

denominator.unit: projected real output and trade-growth frame

business_fixed_investment_2026.unit: percent projected real business fixed-investment growth in 2026

export_growth_2026.unit: percent projected real export growth in 2026

trade_deficit_2036.unit: percent of GDP projected for the trade deficit in 2036

dollar_change.unit: percent projected cumulative decline in the dollar's exchange value from 2026 through 2036

ai_productivity.value: wider adoption of generative AI is expected to support productivity and investment, while requiring substantial data-center, computing, and intellectual-property investment

observations.method: CBO projection of trade flows, exchange rates, business investment, productivity, and AI-related capital formation.
observations.uncertainty: The pace and distribution of AI productivity, supply-chain adjustment, exchange-rate movement, and foreign demand are highly uncertain; projected trade and investment changes do not establish realized reshoring or consumer benefit.
observations.subgroup: US exporters, importers, firms using AI or imported inputs, consumers, workers, investors, and foreign trading partners.
observations.counterinterpretation: A smaller trade deficit or higher investment can reflect adjustment costs, lower imports, currency changes, or concentrated gains rather than broad economic security or self-sufficiency.

related_sources.claim: CBO's January 2025 outlook is the principal comparison baseline referenced in the 2026 forecast revisions.

boundary: This record adds a macro-to-lived-conditions pathway: fiscal support, tariffs, immigration policy, aging, AI investment, trade, and debt jointly shape US growth, prices, labor supply, and household room. It is a CBO forecast under current-law and policy assumptions, not observed outcomes, a causal policy evaluation, or a distributional household panel.
